id: ‘One morn I left him in his bed’

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

One morn I left him in his bed; A moment after some one said, ‘Your child is dying – he is dead.’ We made him ready for his rest, Flowers in his hair, and on his breast His little hands together prest. We sailed by night across the sea; So, floating from the world were we, Apart from sympathy, we Three. The wild sea moaned, the black clouds spread Moving shadows on its bed, But one of us lay midship dead. I saw his coffin sliding down The yellow sand in yonder town, Where I put on my sorrow’s crown. And we returned; in this drear place Never to see him face to face, I thrust aside the living race. Mothers, who mourn with me today, Oh, understand me, when I say, I cannot weep, I cannot pray; I gaze upon a hidden store, His books, his toys, the clothes he wore, And cry, ‘Once more, to me, once more!’ Then take, from me, this simple verse, That you may know what I rehearse— A grief – your and my Universe!

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

* A parent experiences the sudden death of their young child and prepares his body for burial.
* The family travels across the sea by night to lay the child's coffin to rest in a distant town.
* Upon returning home, the parent isolates themselves from society, deeply paralyzed by sorrow and unable to weep or pray.
* The parent clings to the child's remaining belongings, such as his books and toys, desperately longing to see him again.
* The speaker shares this poem with other mourning mothers to acknowledge the universal bond of a parent's grief.

Here are two ways to polish this text while preserving every detail and emotion of the original. 

### Option 1: Poetic & Refined (Preserving Verse)
*This option maintains the poetic structure and tragic beauty of the original while improving meter, flow, and literary elegance.*

> One morning, I left him resting in his bed;  
> A moment later, the words were said:  
> “Your child is dying—he is dead.”  
> 
> We prepared his body for eternal rest,  
> With flowers in his hair and on his chest,  
> His small, tender hands together pressed.  
> 
> By night, we set sail across the sea,  
> Floating away from reality,  
> Untouched by sympathy, just we three.  
> 
> The wild sea moaned as dark clouds spread  
> Shifting shadows on its restless bed,  
> While midship lay our darling, dead.  
> 
> I saw his coffin sliding down  
> The yellow sand of a distant town,  
> Where I first put on my sorrow’s crown.  
> 
> We returned to a desolate place, knowing full well  
> I would never again gaze upon his face,  
> And so I withdrew from the living race.  
> 
> To the mothers who mourn alongside me today,  
> Please understand me when I say:  
> I cannot weep, I cannot pray.  
> 
> I only gaze upon his hidden store—  
> His books, his toys, the clothes he wore—  
> And cry, “Return to me, just once more!”  
> 
> Pray, accept from me this simple verse,  
> That you may share what I rehearse:  
> A sorrow that boundlessly fills our universe.

---

### Option 2: Eloquent Prose (For Essays, Speeches, or Memoirs)
*This option converts the narrative into polished, deeply moving, professional prose while retaining every single element of the original story.*

> One morning, I left him resting in his bed, only to be told moments later that he was dying—and then, that he was gone. We prepared his body for eternal rest, placing flowers in his hair and upon his chest, his small hands gently pressed together. That night, we journeyed across the sea, drifting away from the world and beyond the reach of human comfort—just the three of us. As dark clouds cast shifting shadows over the moaning waves, he lay motionless in the midship. In a distant town, I watched his coffin slide down into the golden sand, the precise moment I took upon myself the heavy crown of sorrow. 
>
> Upon returning to this dreary place, knowing I would never see his face again, I turned my back entirely on the living world. To all the mothers who mourn alongside me today, please understand: I find myself unable to weep, unable to pray. I can only gaze upon his preserved belongings—his books, his toys, the clothes he once wore—and cry out into the silence, “Just once more, return to me!” Please accept this simple verse as a testament to my story, a reflection of the shared grief that has become our entire universe.
outputs.L2:
Here is a rewrite of the passage, keeping all of the original details and narrative sequence while using entirely new phrasing and prose structure:

***

Early one morning, I left my young boy resting in his bed, only to be told moments later that he was gravely ill—and then, that he had passed away. We prepared his body for eternal sleep, weaving blossoms into his hair and folding his small hands over his chest. 

Under the cover of night, we set sail across the sea. Out on the water, isolated from human comfort, the three of us drifted far from the rest of the world. Darkness stretched across the sky as shifting clouds cast shadows over the wailing waves, while the lifeless boy lay in the middle of the ship. Upon arriving at a distant coastal town, I watched his casket descend into the golden earth, marking the moment my supreme heartache was sealed.

Afterward, we made our way back. Now trapped in a bleak reality where I will never look upon his face again, I shun the company of the living. 

To all the fellow mothers who share my anguish, I ask you to understand my plight: my sorrow is so overwhelming that I am unable to cry or even pray. Instead, I fix my eyes on a hidden collection of his belongings—his reading materials, playthings, and garments—desperately pleading for just one more moment with him. 

Please accept these humble words I offer, so you may realize what I endure every day: a profound loss that encompasses the entire world for both you and me.
outputs.L3:
The world changes in a single, devastating breath when a parent is forced to confront the sudden death of their young child. Stripped of the future they had imagined, the grieving parent must undertake the heartbreaking duty of preparing their child’s small body for the grave. In quiet, agonizing tenderness, they bathe and clothe the silent form, performing a final act of devotion for a life cut tragically short.

Under the shroud of a moonlit night, the family sets out on a solemn journey, traveling across dark, quiet seas to lay the child to rest in a distant town. The rhythmic sway of the ship and the vast emptiness of the ocean reflect the profound isolation of their loss. Arriving at their destination, they surrender the small coffin to the earth, leaving behind a piece of their own souls in the cold ground before beginning the hollow journey back.

Upon returning to a home now defined by absence, the parent retreats completely from society. Paralyzed by the sheer weight of sorrow, they shut out the rest of the world. In this stagnant darkness, grief manifests not in loud lamentations, but in a terrible, frozen silence; the parent finds themselves unable to weep to release the pressure in their heart, nor can they find solace in prayer, feeling entirely abandoned by faith.

In this deep isolation, the child’s remaining belongings become sacred relics. The parent moves through the quiet rooms, clinging desperately to his dog-eared books, his forgotten toys, and the small objects his hands once touched. These simple items become tangible bridges to a lost paradise, fueling an overwhelming, unbearable longing to see his face, hear his voice, and hold him just once more.

Yet, out of this unspeakable despair, a fragile connection to humanity emerges. The speaker channels this unimaginable pain into written verse, offering the poem as a vessel of solace for other mourning mothers. In sharing this deeply personal tragedy, the narrative transcends individual heartbreak, forging a quiet, empathetic sanctuary that acknowledges the universal, unbreakable bond of a parent’s grief.
outputs.L4:
Here is an expansion of the summary into a complete, poetic prose text:

***

There is a cold violence in the distance that now separates us. The earth opened and closed so suddenly, taking my sweet boy into a soil I cannot reach, laying him to rest beneath a horizon far beyond the touch of my seeking hands. He was here, vibrant and warm, and then the world shattered; now he sleeps in a distant grave, while I am left behind in a home that has suddenly turned into a silent, cavernous tomb. 

In the suffocating quiet of these rooms, his memory is preserved not in grand monuments, but in the small, agonizing remnants of his ordinary life. I stand paralyzed before a pair of tiny, scuffed shoes left beside the doorway, still holding the shape of his restless little feet. I touch a half-finished drawing left upon the table, a wooden toy abandoned on the rug, a small coat hanging from a peg—inanimate objects that have outlived the fleeting light of my child. They are cruel relics of a future stolen away, monuments to a presence that filled every corner of my existence.

They tell me to seek solace in faith, to fold my hands and lift my voice to the heavens. But when I try to pray, my mouth fills with ash. The sky above feels hollow, indifferent, and vast; no words can bridge the chasm between my desolate heart and a God who permitted such a theft. They tell me that tears will bring relief, yet my eyes remain dry, scorched by the heat of a desperate, unyielding longing. My grief is too profound for tears, too heavy for prayer. It sits within my chest like a stone, a silent, unmoving weight that refuses the comfort of weeping.

And so, deprived of tears and stripped of prayer, I turn my voice to you—the quiet legion of mothers who walk this same dark valley. You who know the excruciating weight of an empty nursery, who listen for a phantom laughter in the hallway, who carry the heavy silence of a child’s absence. I address you not to offer platitudes or promises of healing, but to extend a hand across the void. We are bound together by an agony that language can barely contain, drawn into a quiet sisterhood forged in the crucible of loss.

Let these words stand as a testament for us all. If I cannot pray, let this verse be my altar. If I cannot weep, let these lines carry the weight of the tears we cannot shed. Grief is an all-encompassing universe—a dark, infinite expanse inhabited by every heart that has ever mourned a child. Within its borders, we are never truly healed, but in the echo of each other’s sorrow, we are no longer entirely alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a tragic Victorian-style narrative poem in rhymed tercets about a mother who loses her young son, sails across the sea to bury him, and is left in perpetual grief.
counterfactuals.output:
The tallow lamp burned down to ghostly grey,
As from his frame the sweet soul slipped away,
And left her child a form of lifeless clay.

She bound his golden hair with ribbon true,
And kissed his cheek of cold and marble hue,
Where late the rosy light of morning grew.

No doctor’s art could turn the creeping chill,
Nor wake the quiet heart that lay so still;
She bowed beneath the Lord’s relentless will.

"Across the sea thy resting place be made,
Where in ancestral earth thou shalt be laid,
Beneath the ancient headland’s quiet shade."

They bore the little coffin to the ship,
A prayer of sorrow trembling on her lip,
While salty mists did from the rigging drip.

The black bark sailed into the surging night,
O'er ink-black waves untouched by starry light,
While she kept vigil till the dawn grew white.

The gale blew fierce, the bitter spray flew high,
An echo to her desolate, wild cry,
Beneath a vast and unresponding sky.

At length they reached the bleak and rocky strand,
Where mournful breakers beat the barren land,
To lay the child upon his father's sand.

They lowered down the box of polished oak,
While through the gloom no word of comfort spoke,
And in her breast the final anchor broke.

She knelt upon the cold and weeping sod,
And gave her single treasure up to God,
Then back toward the sea she slowly trod.

Now decades drift like shadows on the deep,
Yet in her heart she guards his silent sleep,
A pale, grey ghost who has no tears to weep.

Her black crepe veil is worn, her hair is grey,
She sits forever by the stormy bay,
And mourns the little son she laid away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a sad poem about a mother grieving her dead child.
counterfactuals.output:
The mobile hangs still in the draft of the door,
Cast in a shadow that sleeps on the floor.
The yellow wooden blocks lie half-piled in a row,
Exactly as left in the soft long-ago.

I walk through the nursery, silent and cold,
To touch the small blanket I used to unfold.
The scent of baby soap is fading away,
Stolen by hours, devoured by the day.

My arms are so heavy, yet hollow inside,
A well full of grief where my heart used to hide.
At midnight I wake to a phantom-like cry,
And reach for the air with a desperate sigh.

My body remembers the weight of your head,
The warmth of your breath as I tucked you in bed.
Now all of my instincts are burdens I bear—
A mother’s deep love with no child to receive it there.

The sun has the nerve to keep rising each dawn,
Uncaring that all of my light is now gone.
I sing to the quiet, a lullaby low,
To the sweetest little soul that I had to let go. 

I will carry your absence, a stone in my chest,
A whisper of joy that was laid into rest.
Until the dark closes, and time sets me free,
I will hold you in dreams, till you hold me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you compose an elegy from the perspective of a grieving parent? Include details about carrying the child's coffin across the ocean by night, returning home to his untouched toys and clothes, and feeling unable to pray.
counterfactuals.output:
The ocean held no bottom, held no shore,
As through the moonless black we carved our way.
I carried you, who walked with me before,
Confined in polished oak, away from day.

Beneath the groaning deck, in salt and chill,
I kept my vigil by your narrow box.
The hull roared on, but you lay terrible and still,
Indifferent to the dark sea’s heavy shocks.

My hands, which used to lift you to the sky,
To swing you high above the garden wall,
Now braced the weight where all my treasures lie,
And learned how heavy is a child so small.

At last, we brought you back across the deep,
To tread the threshold of this ruined hall,
Where time itself has fallen fast asleep,
And shadows lengthen on the parlor wall.

Here wait your small, untouched, abandoned things:
The tin lead soldiers frozen mid-command,
The wooden bird with painted, motionless wings,
The little sweater waiting for your hand.

Your small leather boots still gather quiet dust
Beside the bed where last you turned and played.
I breathe the ghost of you, as parents must,
And touch the impression that your body made.

They whisper I should bow my head and pray,
To seek for solace from a holy light—
But all my sacred words have rotted away,
And choked within a mouth as dry as night.

I try to kneel, but stone is all I feel;
No psalm can reach the depth of my despair.
I hold your quiet coat against the dark,
And find no God within the empty air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a 19th-century style poem using AAA rhyming triplets that explores the deep, isolating sorrow of losing a child and ends with a message to other mourning mothers.
counterfactuals.output:
The hearth is cold where once thy laughter played,
In quiet ground my sweetest hope is laid,
And all my world is cast in bitter shade.

The shadows gather where the lonely weep,
While locked within a dreamless, endless sleep,
Thou art entombed in silence dark and deep.

The autumn wind laments across the plain,
My heart is heavy with a constant pain,
And all my calling calls to thee in vain.

The busy world moves on, nor heeds my moan;
I walk the icy paths of grief alone,
My bleeding soul turned cold as dampened stone.

Yet ye who walk this night of heavy sorrow,
Ye grieving mothers of a sunless morrow,
Whose wounded spirits can no comfort borrow:

Know that ye tread no solitary shore,
Our tears unite until the night is o’er,
And love shall claim its treasure evermore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a poem where a mother recounts the sudden death of her little boy, traveling to a distant town for his burial, and coping with her grief back home. Use somewhat archaic phrasing like "morn," "yonder," and "drear."
counterfactuals.output:
The sunlight kissed his laughing brow that morn,
No shadow warned he would be snatched away;
Ere twilight fell, my bleeding heart was torn,
And pale as snow my little darling lay.

So swift the fever claimed his tender breath,
No earthly art his fleeting life could save;
The bright young day was swallowed up in death,
And all my world became a sudden grave.

We bore him far across the misty moor,
To yonder town where ancient willows weep;
A mournful journey to a distant shore,
To lay my sweetest lamb in final sleep.

The churchyard soil was dark with falling rain,
The autumn wind blew bitter, cold, and drear;
They lowered down my hope, my joy, my pain,
And left him in the silence sleeping there.

Now to this empty home I turn once more,
Where ghostly stillness reigns in every room;
His tiny shoes still wait beside the door,
Unclaimed and silent in the gathering gloom.

When sorrow wakes me at the break of morn,
My vacant arms reach out to clasp his frame;
Methinks I hear his merry voice, upborne
Upon the breeze—yet none doth speak his name.

Though yonder lies the sod that guards his rest,
And weary miles now stretch between us two,
I press his little garment to my breast,
And bide the dark hours till I join him, too.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
